title: GlobalFoundries to Build Two Chip Plants With Up to $21 Billion Funding
source_used: Associated Press (via News-Herald), plus Seoul Economic Daily relaying Bloomberg and Truth Social
key_facts: GlobalFoundries said on Wednesday 14 Oct 2026 it plans two factories in Malta, New York, financed by up to $21 billion from Japan.
The deal was made possible by the Trump administration's trade and investment agreement with Japan.
About $10 billion would speed construction of a factory to open in 2029 and about $10 billion would fund a second plant.
President Trump posted that the US government will receive shares in GlobalFoundries, as it did with Intel; Bloomberg (via Seoul Economic Daily) says about 4 percent.

Federal money previously promised to GlobalFoundries will go to other projects; Seoul Economic Daily says $955 million of CHIPS Act subsidies go to silicon photonics, silicon germanium and advanced packaging.
Bloomberg says the plants will make chips for cars, industrial equipment and telecoms equipment.
GlobalFoundries chief executive Tim Breen said the plants would raise US wafer capacity by 10 percent.
Trump said the project would create 27,000 construction jobs and over 1,000 manufacturing jobs.
quote_evidence: Computer chip company GlobalFoundries Inc. said Wednesday it plans to open two factories in Malta, New York, financed by an investment of up to $21 billion from Japan.

President Donald Trump posted on social media that the U.S. government will receive shares in GlobalFoundries, just as it did for Intel Corp., in an expansion of the administration’s policy of taking ownership stakes in private companies.
GlobalFoundries said in a statement that roughly $10 billion would accelerate construction of a chip factory to open in 2029 and the other $10 billion would fund a second plant.
why_it_matters_hint: A Japanese-funded expansion of US chip capacity with the US government taking a share.
notes: WSJ original returns HTTP 401 and Reuters shows a JS wall; read AP (News-Herald) and Seoul Economic Daily instead. The pool date of 17 Oct is wrong: WSJ and Reuters ran it on 14 Oct 2026. No edition of 14 to 16 Oct carried the $21 billion story. Event older than the window.
